docs.title: QIMP
docs.text:
Quantum Image Processing on Qiskit, with a modular API and a scalable design.

QIMP implements the three canonical quantum image representations from the literature — FRQI, NEQR, and QPIE — plus the geometric / chromatic operations and the Quantum Hadamard Edge Detection (QHED) algorithm that operate on them. Specifications follow docs/tesi.pdf (Dolciami, Politecnico di Torino, 2022, Chapter 3).

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Scalable by construction. Every encoder accepts arbitrary n (image side = 2^n), q (NEQR intensity qubits), and m (multi-image FRQI). No constants are hard-coded; tests are parametrized over qubit counts.
  • Modern stack. Qiskit ≥ 1.0, Python ≥ 3.10, src/-layout, hatchling build, ruff + mypy strict.
  • Modular. Encoding, processing, runtime, I/O, and testing live in independent sub-packages.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
=== "FRQI (phase encoding)"

```python
import numpy as np
from qimp.encoding.frqi import FrqiEncoder
from qimp.testing import ideal_simulation
from qimp.metrics import psnr

image = np.random.randint(0, 256, (4, 4), dtype=np.uint8)
encoder = FrqiEncoder()
qc = encoder.encode(image)          # 2n + 1 = 5 qubits
counts = ideal_simulation(qc, 40_000)
decoded = encoder.decode(counts)[0]
print("PSNR:", psnr(image, decoded), "dB")
```

=== "NEQR (basis encoding)"

```python
from qimp.encoding.neqr import NeqrEncoder

image = np.array([[10, 20], [30, 40]], dtype=np.int64)
encoder = NeqrEncoder(q=8)
qc = encoder.encode(image)          # 2n + q = 10 qubits
counts = ideal_simulation(qc, 4096)
print(encoder.decode(counts))       # exact recovery
```

=== "QPIE (amplitude encoding)"

```python
from qimp.encoding.qpie import QpieEncoder

encoder = QpieEncoder()
qc = encoder.encode(image.astype(float))   # 2n = 4 qubits
counts = ideal_simulation(qc, 80_000)
print(encoder.decode(counts))
```

=== "QHED (edge detection)"

```python
from qimp.processing.filters import qhed_filter, qhed_full_edges

qc_h, n, rms = qhed_filter(image)
qc_v, _, _ = qhed_filter(image.T)
counts_h = ideal_simulation(qc_h, 40_000)
counts_v = ideal_simulation(qc_v, 40_000)
edges = qhed_full_edges(image, counts_h, counts_v)
```

docs.title: Encodings
docs.text:
Three canonical encodings, three different trade-offs.

Encoding Type Qubits Retrieval Complexity FRQI Phase 2n + 1 Approximated (shot-noise) O(2^{4n}) NEQR Basis 2n + q Exact O(q·n·2^{2n}) QPIE Amplitude 2n Approximated (shot-noise) O(2^n)

docs.title: FRQI — Flexible Representation of Quantum Images
docs.text:
Pixel intensities map to RY rotation angles applied to a color qubit controlled by the position register. Compact (one extra qubit on top of position), but retrieval is approximate and intensity precision is shot-limited.

from qimp.encoding.frqi import FrqiEncoder

encoder = FrqiEncoder()
qc = encoder.encode(image)         # image: (2^n, 2^n)
# ... run, get counts ...
recovered = encoder.decode(counts)[0]

Multi-image FRQI: pass a stack of images ((num_images, H, W)) and m = ⌈log₂(num_images)⌉ selection qubits are added automatically. Non-power-of-two batches are zero-padded.

qc = encoder.encode(np.stack([image_a, image_b]))    # 2n + 1 + 1 qubits

docs.title: NEQR — Novel Enhanced Quantum Representation
docs.text:
Intensity is stored as a basis state in a q-qubit register, conditional on the position register. This gives exact retrieval — useful for arithmetic operations that need precise pixel values.

from qimp.encoding.neqr import NeqrEncoder

encoder = NeqrEncoder(q=8)         # 8-bit intensity, max value 255
qc = encoder.encode(image)         # image: (2^n, 2^n), integer dtype
recovered = encoder.decode(counts)
assert (recovered == image).all()  # byte-for-byte recovery

The cost is the extra q qubits and a higher per-pixel gate count.

docs.title: QPIE — Quantum Probability Image Encoding
docs.text:
Pixel intensities are stored directly as amplitude probabilities: |Ψ⟩ = Σ (I_i / ‖I‖) |i⟩. The most compact encoding (only 2n qubits, no color register), at the cost of an arbitrary state preparation that transpiles to deep circuits.

from qimp.encoding.qpie import QpieEncoder

encoder = QpieEncoder()
qc = encoder.encode(image.astype(float))
recovered = encoder.decode(counts)

Note that QPIE preserves intensity proportions, not absolute scale. The decoder uses the RMS computed at encoding time to rescale back; you only get proportional reconstruction otherwise.

docs.title: Choosing between them
docs.text:
• Need exact pixel values for arithmetic / sorting? → NEQR.
  • Need compact circuits for shallow-depth experiments on near-term hardware? → QPIE.
  • Need the classical interface point for variational pipelines (e.g. QHED-style algorithms)? → QPIE (QHED is QPIE-only).
  • Don't have multi-controlled X gates with auxiliary qubits but accept amplitude encoding of intensity? → FRQI.

docs.title: Qubit layout convention
docs.text:
All three encodings share the same position-register layout:

Qubit indices Role 0 .. n-1 X axis (column). Qubit i holds bit i of the column index (LSB-first). n .. 2n-1 Y axis (row). Qubit n + i holds bit i of the row index (LSB-first). Above 2n Encoding-specific: FRQI color qubit at 2n, NEQR intensity qubits below position (qubits 0..q-1), QPIE has nothing above.

This means that when you read a Qiskit count bitstring (MSB-first), the leftmost bit (after the color/intensity prefix) is the high bit of the row index, and the rightmost is the LSB of the column index. The np.fliplr / np.flipud / np.transpose mapping used by qimp.processing.geometric follows this convention.

For NEQR, position qubits start at offset q (the intensity register occupies qubits 0..q-1). Pass pos_offset=q to any geometric operation.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
All public APIs are parametric in qubit count. You can encode arbitrarily large images (memory permitting) without code changes:

import numpy as np
from qimp.encoding.frqi import FrqiEncoder

# n = 4 → 16x16 image → 2n + 1 = 9 qubits
encoder = FrqiEncoder()
qc = encoder.encode(np.zeros((16, 16), dtype=np.uint8))

# n = 6 → 64x64 image → 2n + 1 = 13 qubits
qc = encoder.encode(np.zeros((64, 64), dtype=np.uint8))

The hard wall is your simulator's RAM (or QPU's qubit count), not the library.

docs.title: Processing
docs.text: Once an image is encoded, processing operations act on its quantum register. QIMP groups them into four sub-modules.

docs.title: Geometric (qimp.processing.geometric)
docs.text:
Pure position-qubit manipulations — encoding-agnostic: the same axis_flip works on FRQI, NEQR, and QPIE circuits, you just pass a pos_offset argument telling it where the position register starts (0 for FRQI / QPIE, q for NEQR).

Function Effect axis_flip(qc, n, axis, pos_offset=0) Flip along X or Y axis coord_swap(qc, n, pos_offset=0) Transpose (swap row ↔ col) ort_rotation(qc, n, angle, pos_offset=0) 90° / 180° / 270° rotation pos_shift(qc, n, axis, direction, magnitude, pos_offset=0) Cyclic shift restr_flip(qc, n, axis, region_bits, pos_offset=0) Flip a sub-region restr_coord_swap(qc, n, region_bits, pos_offset=0) Transpose a sub-region 
from qimp.encoding.neqr import neqr_circuit, neqr_decode
from qimp.processing.geometric import axis_flip

qc = neqr_circuit(image, q=8)
axis_flip(qc, n=2, axis="y", pos_offset=8)   # flip horizontally (X axis)
# ... measure, decode ...

End-to-end semantics are verified by encoding with NEQR (exact retrieval), applying the op, decoding, and comparing against the numpy reference (np.fliplr, np.transpose, np.rot90, np.roll).

docs.title: Chromatic (qimp.processing.chromatic)
docs.text:
Encoding-specific intensity manipulations.

Function Encoding Effect frqi_color_complement(qc) FRQI θ → π − θ on color qubit frqi_color_change(qc, theta) FRQI rotate intensities by θ neqr_color_complement(qc, q) NEQR bit-flip all intensity qubits → (2^q − 1) − I neqr_half_intensity(qc, q) NEQR right-shift intensity bits neqr_classify_complement(qc, q, threshold_bit) NEQR flip bits below the threshold

docs.title: Filters (qimp.processing.filters)
docs.text:
Currently exposes the QHED (Quantum Hadamard Edge Detection) algorithm, the showcase application of the thesis: detect edges with only 2n + 1 qubits using H gates and a cyclic decrement on an auxiliary register.

from qimp.processing.filters import qhed_filter, qhed_decode, qhed_full_edges
from qimp.testing import ideal_simulation

# Horizontal gradients
qc, n, rms = qhed_filter(image)
counts = ideal_simulation(qc, shots=40_000)
edges_h = qhed_decode(counts, n=n, rms=rms)

# Full edge map (horizontal + vertical via transposed image)
qc_v, _, _ = qhed_filter(image.T)
counts_v = ideal_simulation(qc_v, shots=40_000)
edges = qhed_full_edges(image, counts, counts_v)

QHED is not a pure horizontal-only filter

The QHED implementation runs a single cyclic decrement on the combined aux+position register. The resulting adjacency is row-major Z-curve: pixel (r, 2^n − 1) is considered adjacent to (r + 1, 0). This creates spurious "edges" at the last column of every row. Inspect the output carefully — at minimum, mask out the last column before visualising; for true row-only gradients, post-process classically.

docs.text: The Streamlit-based QIMP Explorer lets you exercise every encoder and every processing operation, plus the GP-ratio pipeline, without writing code.

docs.title: The wizard (app.py)
docs.text:
The main page is a sequential 5-step wizard. Each step unlocks the next:

  1. Load — upload a TIFF/PNG or pick a file from data/immagini/. Shows the raw preview (NEAREST-neighbor upscaled so small images stay crisp).
  2. Preprocess — optionally resize the image to a power-of-two side (2, 4, 8, 16, 32, or 64 px) and / or convert RGB → grayscale (BT.601 luma).
  3. Encode — pick FRQI / NEQR / QPIE / MCRQI / NCQI, choose intensity-qubit counts where applicable, then build the circuit. Reports qubits, pre- and post-transpile depth.
  4. Process (optional) — chain geometric (flip, swap, rotate) and chromatic (color complement, half intensity) operations. After every applied op the wizard runs a quick 8 k-shot ideal simulation, decodes it, and shows the input image next to the after-image so you can chain ops visually. A Reset ops button rebuilds the freshly-encoded circuit.
  5. Execute & Export — run the final circuit on the local simulator (ideal or noisy), or copy the OpenQASM 3 snippet, or submit directly to an IBM Quantum backend via the Sampler primitive (paste API token in the sidebar — token stays in session memory only, never persisted).

Every save action writes TIFFs to data/output/run_<timestamp>/.

docs.title: Add-on pages (sidebar)
docs.text: Page What you can do Benchmark Run all three encoders on the same image; sortable pandas table (PSNR + TV + depth + runtime) + bar charts. GP-ratio Microscopy pipeline: classical GP image in all 3 output formats (normalized / uint8 / 16-bit), optional Gaussian + median preprocessing, and parametric quantum circuit construction. System Info Library / Qiskit / Python versions, simulator backend (GPU detection), dataset stats, past-run inventory, cache-clearing buttons.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• FRQI above n = 3 is impractical because of the multi-controlled RY gates. Use the Preprocess step to resize to 4×4 or 8×8 first.
  • NEQR is exact: with enough shots the round-trip is bit-perfect.
  • The full GP-ratio optimisation loop is intentionally not run in the UI (it takes 10+ minutes per image on a CPU simulator). The page builds the parametric circuit and reports depth / gate counts; use a notebook for the full COBYLA optimisation.

docs.title: qimp.encoding.frqi
docs.text:
FRQI encoding: Flexible Representation of Quantum Images.

A 2^n × 2^n grayscale image is encoded into 2n+1 qubits: 2n position qubits plus 1 color qubit. The pixel intensity is mapped to an RY rotation angle and applied via a fully-controlled RY gate. Multiple images can be stacked by adding m = ceil(log2(num_images)) selection qubits, for a total of 2n+m+1 qubits.

Scales freely with n (image side = 2^n) and m (number of stacked images = 2^m).

Reference: docs/tesi.pdf §3.1.1, §2.2.1

docs.title: FrqiEncoder
docs.text:
Stateful FRQI encoder.

Bundles the normalization factor and inferred n/m so the same instance can be reused for encode→measure→decode round-trips.

docs.title: frqi_circuit
docs.text:
frqi_circuit(images: ndarray | Sequence[ndarray], *, normalization: float | None = None) -> QuantumCircuit

Build an FRQI quantum circuit for one or more square images.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default images ndarray | Sequence[ndarray]

A single 2D image (shape (2^n, 2^n)), a 3D stack (shape (num_images, 2^n, 2^n)), or a sequence of 2D images. When more than one image is supplied, num_images is padded with zero images to the next power of two and m = log2(num_images_padded) selection qubits are added.

required normalization float | None

Intensity that maps to angle π (full color amplitude on |1⟩). Defaults to the max value of the dtype (255 for uint8, 65535 for uint16, 1.0 for float).

None

Returns:

Type Description QuantumCircuit

Circuit with 2n + m + 1 qubits and an equal number of classical bits. No measurement gates are appended; call ideal_simulation / device_test on the returned circuit (they add measurements automatically).

docs.title: frqi_decode
docs.text:
frqi_decode(counts: dict[str, int], n: int, m: int = 0, normalization: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray | list[np.ndarray]

Decode measurement counts from an FRQI circuit into one or more images.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default counts dict[str, int]

Qiskit-style histogram from ideal_simulation(qc, shots).

required n int

Number of spatial qubits per axis (image side = 2^n).

required m int

Number of selection qubits (number of images = 2^m). Defaults to 0 (single image).

0 normalization float

Intensity that maps to θ = π — must match what was used at encoding. The reconstructed intensity for pixel j of image s is prob(color=1 | pos=j, sel=s) * normalization.

1.0

Returns:

Type Description ndarray | list[ndarray]
  • When m == 0 (single image): a single (2^n, 2^n) float array, matching the shape contract of neqr_decode / qpie_decode.
  • When m > 0: a list of 2^m images, since only FRQI supports multi-image encoding via image-selection qubits.

docs.title: intensities_to_angles
docs.text:
intensities_to_angles(intensities: ndarray, normalization: float) -> np.ndarray

Map pixel intensities to RY angles in [0, π].

Convention: intensity 0 → θ = 0, intensity = normalization → θ = π. After RY(θ), prob(color qubit = 1) = sin²(θ/2) = intensity / normalization.

docs.title: qimp.encoding.neqr
docs.text:
NEQR encoding: Novel Enhanced Quantum Representation.

A 2^n × 2^n grayscale image with intensity resolution 2^q is encoded into 2n + q qubits. The intensity is stored in a separate q-bit register (basis-state encoding), enabling exact retrieval and arithmetic operations.

Qubit layout (low → high index): - q intensity qubits (qubits 0 … q-1) - n X-position qubits (qubits q … q+n-1) - n Y-position qubits (qubits q+n … q+2n-1)

Reference: docs/tesi.pdf §2.2.2, §3.1.2

docs.title: NeqrEncoder
docs.text: Stateful NEQR encoder that records n and q for round-trips.

docs.title: neqr_circuit
docs.text:
neqr_circuit(image: ndarray, q: int = 8) -> QuantumCircuit

Build a NEQR circuit for a single grayscale image.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default image ndarray

Square (2^n, 2^n) integer array with values in [0, 2^q - 1].

required q int

Number of intensity qubits. Image values must fit in q bits.

8

Returns:

Type Description QuantumCircuit

Circuit with 2n + q qubits.

Notes

Complexity: O(q · n · 2^(2n)) gates worst-case. Scales freely with both n and q.

docs.title: neqr_decode
docs.text:
neqr_decode(counts: dict[str, int], n: int, q: int) -> np.ndarray

Decode NEQR measurement counts into the reconstructed image.

For each position, the most-frequent intensity reading is taken (NEQR is exact, so ideal simulations yield a single intensity per pixel).

docs.title: qimp.encoding.qpie
docs.text:
QPIE encoding: Quantum Probability Image Encoding.

Pixel intensities are normalized so that their squared values sum to 1, then loaded as amplitude probabilities into 2n qubits via Qiskit's initialize. Compact (only 2n qubits) but produces an arbitrary state preparation that transpiles to deep circuits.

Reference: docs/tesi.pdf §2.2.3, §3.1.3

docs.title: QpieEncoder
docs.text: Stateful QPIE encoder that records n and the RMS for decoding.

docs.title: qpie_circuit
docs.text:
qpie_circuit(image: ndarray) -> QuantumCircuit

Build a QPIE circuit for a single grayscale image.

The circuit has 2n qubits; the state is |Ψ⟩ = Σ_i (I_i / ‖I‖) |i⟩ where |i⟩ is the position basis state.

Scales freely with n. The intensity resolution is bounded only by the number of measurement shots (no q parameter — QPIE has no intensity register).

docs.title: qpie_decode
docs.text:
qpie_decode(counts: dict[str, int], n: int, rms: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray

Decode QPIE measurement counts into a reconstructed image.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default counts dict[str, int]

Histogram from ideal_simulation(qpie_circuit(image), shots).

required n int

Number of spatial qubits per axis (image side = 2^n).

required rms float

Root-mean-square of the original intensities, √(mean(I²)). Returned by QpieEncoder.encode(); if unknown, leave 1.0 to recover the normalized image (the absolute scale of QPIE is not preserved).

1.0

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

(2^n, 2^n) float array; I_yx ≈ √(N_yx / N_meas) · RMS·√(2^(2n)). Multiplying by √(2^(2n)) cancels the 1/√M factor implicit in the amplitude normalisation.

docs.title: qimp.processing.geometric
docs.text:
Geometric transformations on encoded quantum images.

These operations manipulate position qubits only and therefore apply identically to FRQI, NEQR, and QPIE. The caller supplies n (qubits per spatial axis) and an offset that points to the first position qubit in the target circuit:

============ ================================= Encoding Position-qubit offset ============ ================================= FRQI 0 (qubits 0..2n-1) QPIE 0 (qubits 0..2n-1) NEQR q (qubits q..q+2n-1, with q the intensity-qubit count) ============ =================================

Qubit layout within the position block (LSB-first): - pos_offset .. pos_offset + n - 1 → X-axis qubits (column, x_0 … x_{n-1}) - pos_offset + n .. pos_offset + 2n - 1 → Y-axis qubits (row, y_0 … y_{n-1})

Reference: docs/tesi.pdf §2.3

docs.title: axis_flip
docs.text:
axis_flip(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, axis: Axis, *, pos_offset: int = 0) -> QuantumCircuit

Flip the image about the given axis.

axis='x' flips about the X axis (inverts Y / row coordinate) by applying X gates to the Y-axis qubits. axis='y' flips about the Y axis (inverts X / column coordinate) by applying X gates to the X-axis qubits.

Complexity: O(n) X gates.

docs.title: coord_swap
docs.text:
coord_swap(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, *, pos_offset: int = 0) -> QuantumCircuit

Swap row and column coordinates: image transpose.

Applies n SWAP gates between paired position qubits (x_i, y_i). Complexity: O(n) SWAPs ≡ 3n CNOTs.

docs.title: ort_rotation
docs.text:
ort_rotation(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, angle: int, *, pos_offset: int = 0) -> QuantumCircuit

Rotate the image by 90°, 180°, or 270° counter-clockwise.

Decomposition into flip + swap:

  • 90°: coord_swap then axis_flip('y') (swap rows/cols, then invert cols)
  • 180°: axis_flip('x') then axis_flip('y')
  • 270°: coord_swap then axis_flip('x')

Reference: docs/tesi.pdf §2.3.3

docs.title: pos_shift
docs.text:
pos_shift(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, axis: Axis, *, direction: Literal['+', '-'] = '+', magnitude: int = 1, pos_offset: int = 0) -> QuantumCircuit

Shift the image by magnitude pixels along axis.

Implemented as a cyclic increment / decrement on the n-qubit position register for that axis. Each cyclic step is a cascade of multi-controlled X gates of decreasing arity (Toffoli-tower), giving O(n²) gate complexity.

Reference: docs/tesi.pdf §2.3.5

docs.title: restr_flip
docs.text:
restr_flip(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, axis: Axis, region_bits: str, *, pos_offset: int = 0) -> QuantumCircuit

Flip only the pixels whose position prefix matches region_bits.

Each character of region_bits selects a higher-order qubit of the axis being preserved (the axis not being flipped). For example, with n=4 and region_bits="10" on axis='y': flip the column coordinate only for rows whose two MSBs are 10 (i.e. rows 8..11).

Implemented as a multi-controlled X on each X-axis qubit, with controls on the higher-order qubits of the orthogonal axis taking the prefix as a bitmask.

Reference: docs/tesi.pdf §2.3.4

docs.title: restr_coord_swap
docs.text:
restr_coord_swap(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, region_bits: str, *, pos_offset: int = 0) -> QuantumCircuit

Coord-swap restricted to a region selected by region_bits.

Decomposition idea: for each i, apply a controlled-SWAP between x_i and y_i conditioned on the region prefix. Implemented as CSWAP = CNOT(b,a) → Toffoli(ctrl..., a, b) → CNOT(b, a) per pair.

Reference: docs/tesi.pdf §2.3.4

docs.text:
Chromatic transformations: color complement, color change, halving, classify.

Reference: docs/tesi.pdf §2.4

docs.title: frqi_color_complement
docs.text:
frqi_color_complement(qc: QuantumCircuit, *, color_qubit: int | None = None) -> QuantumCircuit

Invert FRQI colors by applying an X to the color qubit.

Maps cos(θ)|0⟩ + sin(θ)|1⟩ → sin(θ)|0⟩ + cos(θ)|1⟩, i.e. θ → π−θ. If color_qubit is None the highest-indexed qubit is used.

docs.title: frqi_color_change
docs.text:
frqi_color_change(qc: QuantumCircuit, theta: float, *, color_qubit: int | None = None) -> QuantumCircuit

Apply a custom unitary on the FRQI color qubit, parameterised by theta.

The unitary is [[cos(θ/2), sin(θ/2)], [sin(θ/2), -cos(θ/2)]] — a reflection matrix that maps cos(α)|0⟩ + sin(α)|1⟩ → cos(α+θ)|0⟩ + sin(α+θ)|1⟩, shifting every pixel intensity by θ modulo π.

docs.title: neqr_color_complement
docs.text:
neqr_color_complement(qc: QuantumCircuit, q: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Bit-wise NOT of every intensity bit: maps i → (2^q − 1) − i for each pixel.

Applies an X gate to each of the q intensity qubits (assumed to be the lowest-indexed q qubits, per the NEQR layout).

docs.title: neqr_half_intensity
docs.text:
neqr_half_intensity(qc: QuantumCircuit, q: int, *, allow_reset: bool = False) -> QuantumCircuit

Divide every pixel intensity by 2 (integer division) by right-shifting one bit.

Implemented as a cascade of SWAPs that re-labels intensity qubits and a final reset of the freed top bit. Effectively maps b_{q-1}…b_1 b_0 → 0 b_{q-1}…b_1.

Hardware note

The final qc.reset(q-1) is non-unitary: on a real device it implies a mid-circuit measurement + conditional X, which is not supported on many IBM backends and breaks composability with downstream unitary operations.

Pass allow_reset=True to acknowledge this and produce the textbook circuit. The default (allow_reset=False) raises rather than silently emitting a non-unitary op; use the SWAP-only cascade if you intend to run on hardware — the freed top bit will then carry whatever was there before the call (garbage if not pre-zeroed, but the circuit stays unitary).

Superposition caveat

After the SWAP cascade, qubit q-1 holds the original LSB of the intensity register, which is generally entangled with the position register on a real image. qc.reset(q-1) then projects that qubit onto |0⟩, which drops the pixel branches where the original LSB was 1. The textbook i → i // 2 map therefore only holds exactly for images with all-even intensities; on arbitrary images, half-intensity must be implemented via mid-circuit measurement + classical-conditional X (post-selection on the LSB), which the current implementation does not provide.

docs.title: neqr_classify_complement
docs.text:
neqr_classify_complement(qc: QuantumCircuit, q: int, threshold_bit: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Binary classification: complement intensity bits below a threshold bit.

Flips every intensity bit at index < threshold_bit. Useful for coarse thresholding workflows.

docs.title: qimp.processing.filters
docs.text:
Quantum filters for spatial processing.

Currently exposes the Quantum Hadamard Edge Detection (QHED) algorithm for images encoded with QPIE. QHED is a poly(n) algorithm that uses a single auxiliary qubit, a Hadamard gate, and a cyclic decrement gate to extract gradient information from adjacent pixels in a single shot batch.

Reference: docs/tesi.pdf §2.7.3, §3.1.4

docs.title: qhed_filter
docs.text:
qhed_filter(image: ndarray) -> tuple[QuantumCircuit, int, float]

Build a QHED circuit that exposes adjacent-pixel gradients of image.

The circuit has 2n + 1 qubits:

  • qubit 0: auxiliary qubit (LSB)
  • qubits 1..2n: position register holding the QPIE-encoded image

After execution, measuring with aux = 1 at position i gives a magnitude proportional to |c_i − c_{i+1}| where c are the QPIE amplitudes in row-major flattened order.

.. warning:: This is not a pure horizontal-only gradient. The cyclic decrement acts on the full register modulo 2^{2n+1}, so adjacency wraps around at every row boundary: pixel (r, 2^n − 1) is adjacent to pixel (r + 1, 0) in the flattened representation. The output therefore contains spurious "edges" at the last column of every row, which reflect the wrap-around, not the image. For a pure horizontal-only filter, transpose the image and run QHED on the transposed version, then compose horizontally / vertically yourself and discard the boundary columns.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default image ndarray

Square (2^n, 2^n) non-negative intensity array.

required

Returns:

Type Description qc

The QHED circuit (no measurements appended).

n

Spatial qubits per axis.

rms

Root-mean-square of the input intensities, √(mean(I²)). Forward this to qhed_decode to recover the absolute gradient scale.

Notes

Complexity is O(poly(n)) after Hadamard + Toffoli decomposition, excluding the QPIE initialize which dominates and is itself O(2^{2n}) in depth.

docs.text:
qhed_decode(counts: dict[str, int], n: int, rms: float = 1.0, *, max_gradient: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray

required n int

If given, clip the output to [0, max_gradient].

None

(2^n, 2^n) float array of horizontal gradient magnitudes. Gradients are non-negative; the sign is lost because we measure P(aux=1) ∝ (c_i − c_{i+1})².

docs.title: qhed_full_edges
docs.text:
qhed_full_edges(image: ndarray, counts_horizontal: dict[str, int], counts_vertical: dict[str, int], *, max_gradient: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray

Combine horizontal and vertical gradients into a single edge map.

Typical workflow::

qc_h, n, rms = qhed_filter(image)
qc_v, _, _   = qhed_filter(image.T)
counts_h = ideal_simulation(qc_h, shots=N)
counts_v = ideal_simulation(qc_v, shots=N)
edges    = qhed_full_edges(image, counts_h, counts_v, max_gradient=5.0)

docs.title: qimp.processing.gp_ratio
docs.text:
Green-Purple (GP) ratio computation via a parameterized quantum circuit.

Application module (not part of the core thesis library). Computes (I_G - I_R) / (I_G + I_R) on stacked microscopy channels by encoding the two channels as a multi-image FRQI circuit and using two CRY gates per pixel to write the GP ratio onto an auxiliary color qubit. Parameters are tuned via classical optimisation (scipy.minimize, COBYLA) against the classical GP image.

Migrated from legacy/scripts/gp_quantum_4.py + quantize_analyze_quantum_gp_v3.py. Works for arbitrary n (spatial qubits) and m (image-selection qubits).

docs.title: classical_gp_image
docs.text:
classical_gp_image(image_g: ndarray, image_r: ndarray, *, alpha: float = 1.0, eps: float = 1e-10) -> np.ndarray

Classical Green-Purple ratio: (G − α·R) / (G + α·R) element-wise.

docs.title: apply_gp_function
docs.text:
apply_gp_function(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, m: int, params: Sequence[Parameter | float]) -> QuantumCircuit

Append the parameterised GP sub-circuit in place (per-pixel).

For each of the 2^(2n) pixel positions, two parameters drive:

  1. a fully-controlled RY on the green branch (position matches + selection qubit = 1) writing onto the color qubit (the "G half"),
  2. a fully-controlled RY on the red branch (position matches + selection qubit = 0) writing onto the same color qubit (the "R half"), followed by an unconditional Hadamard that interferes the two channel amplitudes.

Splitting the two rotations across the two selection branches is what makes the per-pixel parameter pair non-degenerate: had both rotations sat on the same selection branch, they would compose into a single RY(θ₁+θ₂) and the model would have only one effective parameter per pixel. (Older versions of this function also missed the position-matching controls — the X-flip mask was applied but the CRY took only selection_qubit as control, so every pixel branch produced the same rotation. Both bugs are fixed.)

The circuit assumes the standard FRQI layout: n row qubits, n column qubits, m selection qubits, 1 color qubit (color qubit index = 2n+m).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default qc QuantumCircuit

Circuit to modify. Must already encode the FRQI representation of two channels (so it has 2n+m+1 qubits).

required n int

Spatial qubits per axis (so image size = 2^n × 2^n).

required m int

Image-selection qubits (so number of stacked images = 2^m). Must be ≥ 1 for the GP construction (we need a selection qubit to be the extra control).

required params Sequence[Parameter | float]

Sequence of 2 · 2^(2n) parameters. Built externally via [Parameter(f"θ{i}") for i in range(2 * 2**(2*n))] and assigned later with qc.assign_parameters(...).

required

Returns:

Type Description QuantumCircuit

The same qc, mutated in place and returned for chaining.

docs.title: decode_gp_counts
docs.text:
decode_gp_counts(counts: dict[str, int], n: int, m: int = 1) -> np.ndarray

Decode GP-circuit measurement counts into a per-pixel GP image.

Marginalises over the image-selection qubits and computes P(color = 1 | position) for each pixel, then maps the probability from [0, 1] to the canonical [-1, 1] GP range via 2·P - 1.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default counts dict[str, int]

Histogram returned by :func:qimp.testing.ideal_simulation / :func:qimp.testing.exact_counts on a circuit that has had :func:apply_gp_function applied.

required n int

Spatial qubits per axis (image side = 2^n).

required m int

Image-selection qubits used at encoding (default 1 for the typical (R, G) stack).

1

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

(2^n, 2^n) float array of GP values in [-1, 1]. Pixels with zero total counts (unreachable in the measurement) decode to 0.

docs.title: analytical_gp_params
docs.text:
analytical_gp_params(green: ndarray, red: ndarray, *, alpha: float = 1.0, normalization: float | None = None, target: ndarray | None = None) -> np.ndarray

Return the closed-form optimal parameters for :func:apply_gp_function.

With the final Hadamard moved outside the per-pixel loop (see apply_gp_function docstring), each pixel p has an independent two-parameter block and the decoded value is

``GP[p] = −(sin(φ_2 + β_p) + sin(φ_1 + α_p)) / 2``

where φ_1 = arccos(1 − 2·I_1[p]/N) and φ_2 = arccos(1 − 2·I_2[p]/N) are the FRQI angles for the two channels (N is the normalisation used at encoding). Setting GP[p] = target[p] is solved by

``α_p = arcsin(−target[p]) − φ_1``
``β_p = arcsin(−target[p]) − φ_2``

giving the exact circuit output without any numerical optimisation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default green ndarray

Matching-shape (2^n, 2^n) channel arrays. The argument names track the lab-historical (green, red) labels; the function is channel-agnostic and applies to any two intensity bands.

required red ndarray

Matching-shape (2^n, 2^n) channel arrays. The argument names track the lab-historical (green, red) labels; the function is channel-agnostic and applies to any two intensity bands.

required alpha float

Sensitivity correction factor for the second channel (the G-factor of the Generalized Polarization formula). Ignored when an explicit target is supplied.

1.0 normalization float | None

FRQI normalisation. Defaults to max(green.max(), red.max()) — the same value :func:evaluate_gp uses internally.

None target ndarray | None

Optional explicit per-pixel target in [-1, 1]. When supplied, the solver fits the circuit to this target instead of the classical Generalized Polarization image. This is the entry point for the Corollary-1 extensions discussed in the companion paper: any bounded ratiometric operator of the two channels (Fura-2 calcium ratio, FRET efficiency, SNARF pH, NDVI, …) may be supplied as target and the closed form recovers the matching parameters.

None

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

Parameter vector of length 2 · 2^(2n) ready to be passed to :func:apply_gp_function / :func:evaluate_gp. Layout follows the same row-major / pixel-index convention as frqi_circuit.

docs.title: optimize_gp
docs.text:
optimize_gp(green: ndarray, red: ndarray, *, alpha: float = 1.0, max_iter: int = 200, seed: int | None = None, weights: tuple[float, float, float] = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0), exact: bool = True, shots: int = 4096) -> OptimizationResult

Optimise the GP circuit parameters against the classical GP image.

Wires together :func:evaluate_gp (quantum image), :func:classical_gp_image (target), and scipy.optimize.minimize(method="COBYLA"). The default loss is pure MSE; pass non-zero weights to bring in the PSNR / TV terms of :func:combined_objective.

With the per-pixel ansatz fix in :func:apply_gp_function, the model is expressive enough to reproduce the classical GP exactly. Empirically COBYLA converges to MSE → 0 (PSNR ~ 85+ dB) in 50 iterations for n=1 and ~480 for n=2.

Matching-shape square (2^n, 2^n) channels.

required red ndarray

Matching-shape square (2^n, 2^n) channels.

Red-channel weight passed to :func:classical_gp_image (the target).

Cap on COBYLA iterations. Default 200 reaches machine-precision convergence for n ≤ 2; larger images may want 1000+.

200 seed int | None

Optional RNG seed for the initial parameter vector.

None weights tuple[float, float, float]

(α_MSE, β_PSNR, γ_TV) weights for :func:combined_objective. Default (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) (pure MSE) is what reaches the exact target; the PSNR / TV terms are mainly diagnostic.

(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) exact bool

import logging
from typing import Any

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

# Module-level cache for the QiskitRuntimeService singleton. Tests reset
# this to None via the autouse `_reset_singleton` fixture.
_SERVICE: Any = None


def get_service(instance: str | None = None) -> Any:
    """Return the cached `QiskitRuntimeService` instance.

    Reads `~/.qiskit/qiskit-ibm.json` on first call. Raises a clear error
    if no saved credentials are found.
    """
    global _SERVICE
    if _SERVICE is not None:
        return _SERVICE

    try:
        from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService
    except ImportError as exc:
        raise ImportError(
            "qimp.runtime.ibm requires `pip install qimp-mi[ibm]` "
            "(qiskit-ibm-runtime)"
        ) from exc

    try:
        _SERVICE = (
            QiskitRuntimeService(instance=instance)
            if instance
            else QiskitRuntimeService()
        )
    except Exception as exc:
        raise RuntimeError(
            "Could not initialise QiskitRuntimeService — is "
            "~/.qiskit/qiskit-ibm.json present and the token valid? "
            f"Underlying error: {exc}"
        ) from exc

    return _SERVICE


def list_backends() -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    """Return one row per operational backend visible to the saved account.

    Each row: `{name, num_qubits, pending_jobs, operational}`.
    """
    service = get_service() if _SERVICE is None else _SERVICE
    rows: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    for backend in service.backends(operational=True):
        status = backend.status()
        rows.append(
            {
                "name": backend.name,
                "num_qubits": backend.num_qubits,
                "pending_jobs": status.pending_jobs,
                "operational": status.operational,
            }
        )
    return rows

def pick_backend(
    service: Any,
    *,
    min_qubits: int,
    name: str | None = None,
) -> Any:
    """Return a backend with at least `min_qubits` operational qubits.

    If `name` is given, fetches that specific backend; otherwise asks
    the service for `least_busy(operational=True, simulator=False,
    min_num_qubits=min_qubits)`. Raises if the chosen backend doesn't
    meet the qubit budget.
    """
    if name is not None:
        backend = service.backend(name)
    else:
        backend = service.least_busy(
            operational=True, simulator=False, min_num_qubits=min_qubits
        )

    if backend.num_qubits < min_qubits:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Backend {backend.name} has {backend.num_qubits} qubits, "
            f"needs >= {min_qubits}"
        )
    logger.info("Picked backend %s (%d qubits)", backend.name, backend.num_qubits)
    return backend

import json
import os
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit


def _atomic_write_bytes(path: Path, payload: bytes) -> None:
    fd, tmp_name = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=str(path.parent), prefix=".tmp_", suffix=path.suffix)
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "wb") as f:
            f.write(payload)
        os.replace(tmp_name, path)
    except Exception:
        if os.path.exists(tmp_name):
            os.unlink(tmp_name)
        raise


def _atomic_write_text(path: Path, text: str) -> None:
    _atomic_write_bytes(path, text.encode("utf-8"))


def persist_run(
    outdir: Path,
    *,
    label: str,
    pass_name: str,
    circuit: QuantumCircuit,
    transpiled: QuantumCircuit | None,
    counts: dict[str, int],
    metadata: dict[str, Any],
) -> Path:
    """Persist a single run's artifacts under `outdir/runs/<label>_<pass>/`.

    Writes (atomically):
    - `circuit.qpy`    — the un-transpiled circuit
    - `transpiled.qpy` — only when `transpiled is not None` (HW runs)
    - `counts.json`    — dict[str, int]
    - `metadata.json`  — caller-supplied dict (job_id, status, depths, ...)
    """
    import io

    from qiskit import qpy

    run_dir = Path(outdir) / "runs" / f"{label}_{pass_name}"
    run_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    buf = io.BytesIO()
    qpy.dump(circuit, buf)
    _atomic_write_bytes(run_dir / "circuit.qpy", buf.getvalue())

    if transpiled is not None:
        buf = io.BytesIO()
        qpy.dump(transpiled, buf)
        _atomic_write_bytes(run_dir / "transpiled.qpy", buf.getvalue())

    _atomic_write_text(run_dir / "counts.json", json.dumps(counts))
    _atomic_write_text(run_dir / "metadata.json", json.dumps(metadata, default=str))
    return run_dir


def is_run_complete(outdir: Path, label: str, pass_name: str) -> bool:
    """True iff the run dir has a non-empty `counts.json` on disk."""
    counts_path = Path(outdir) / "runs" / f"{label}_{pass_name}" / "counts.json"
    if not counts_path.exists():
        return False
    try:
        return bool(json.loads(counts_path.read_text()))
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return False

def _sampler_v2_cls():
    """Indirection so tests can patch the SamplerV2 import without touching
    the qiskit_ibm_runtime package."""
    from qiskit_ibm_runtime import SamplerV2

    return SamplerV2


def _sampler_options_cls():
    from qiskit_ibm_runtime.options import SamplerOptions

    return SamplerOptions


def _transpile_summary(qc: QuantumCircuit) -> dict[str, Any]:
    depth = qc.depth()
    two_q = sum(1 for instr in qc.data if instr.operation.num_qubits >= 2)
    return {
        "depth": depth,
        "two_q_gate_count": two_q,
        "num_qubits": qc.num_qubits,
    }


def hw_run(
    qc: QuantumCircuit,
    *,
    backend: Any,
    shots: int = 4096,
    mitigation: str = "trex+dd",
    optimization_level: int = 3,
    timeout_s: float = 1200.0,
) -> tuple[dict[str, int], QuantumCircuit, str, dict[str, Any]]:
    """Submit `qc` to `backend` via SamplerV2 with TREX + DD mitigation.

    Returns `(counts, transpiled_qc, job_id, transpile_summary)`.
    """
    from qiskit import transpile

    from qimp.testing import _ensure_measured

    measured = _ensure_measured(qc)
    transpiled = transpile(measured, backend=backend, optimization_level=optimization_level)
    summary = _transpile_summary(transpiled)

    Options = _sampler_options_cls()
    options = Options()
    if mitigation == "trex+dd":
        options.dynamical_decoupling.enable = True
        options.dynamical_decoupling.sequence_type = "XY4"
        options.twirling.enable_measure = True
    elif mitigation == "none":
        pass
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown mitigation {mitigation!r}; expected 'trex+dd' or 'none'")

    Sampler = _sampler_v2_cls()
    sampler = Sampler(mode=backend, options=options)
    job = sampler.run([transpiled], shots=shots)
    job_id = job.job_id()
    logger.info("Submitted job %s on %s", job_id, backend.name)

    result = job.result()
    counts = dict(result[0].data.meas.get_counts())
    return counts, transpiled, job_id, summary

from collections.abc import Callable

import numpy as np
from PIL import Image

@dataclass
class CircuitRecipe:
    """One row of the sweep matrix: circuit + decoder + classical reference."""

    label: str
    encoder: str  # "frqi" | "frqi_multi" | "neqr" | "qpie" | "mcrqi" | "ncqi" | "gp"
    n: int
    q: int
    m: int
    qc: QuantumCircuit
    decoder: Callable[[dict[str, int]], np.ndarray]
    reference: np.ndarray


def _downsample_to_n(img: np.ndarray, *, n: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Lanczos-resample to `(2^n, 2^n)`. Preserves dtype for uint8."""
    side = 1 << n
    if img.ndim == 2:
        pil = Image.fromarray(img).resize((side, side), Image.LANCZOS)
        return np.asarray(pil, dtype=img.dtype)
    if img.ndim == 3 and img.shape[2] in (3, 4):
        pil = Image.fromarray(img[..., :3], mode="RGB").resize((side, side), Image.LANCZOS)
        return np.asarray(pil, dtype=img.dtype)
    raise ValueError(f"unsupported image shape {img.shape}")

def build_recipes(image: np.ndarray, *, n: int, q: int = 2, alpha: float = 0.5) -> list[CircuitRecipe]:
    """Build one CircuitRecipe per encoder.

    Parameters
    ----------
    image
        Source frame. 2D grayscale or 3D RGB. Will be downsampled to 2^n × 2^n.
    n
        Spatial qubits per axis.
    q
        Intensity qubits for NEQR/NCQI (default 2 = NISQ-friendly).
    alpha
        G-factor for the GP recipe.
    """
    if image.ndim == 2:
        gray = _downsample_to_n(image, n=n)
        rgb = np.stack([gray, gray, gray], axis=-1)
    else:
        rgb = _downsample_to_n(image, n=n)
        gray = rgb[..., 1]  # use green channel as grayscale source

    side = 1 << n
    recipes: list[CircuitRecipe] = []

    # --- FRQI single-image ---
    from qimp.encoding.frqi import frqi_circuit, frqi_decode

    norm = float(gray.max()) or 1.0
    qc = frqi_circuit(gray, normalization=norm)
    recipes.append(CircuitRecipe(
        label=f"frqi_n{n}", encoder="frqi", n=n, q=0, m=0,
        qc=qc,
        decoder=lambda counts, _n=n, _norm=norm: frqi_decode(counts, n=_n, m=0, normalization=_norm),
        reference=gray.astype(np.float64),
    ))

    # --- FRQI multi-image (m=1, two channels = R, G) ---
    red = rgb[..., 0]
    green = rgb[..., 1]
    stack = np.stack([red, green], axis=0).astype(np.float64)
    norm_multi = float(stack.max()) or 1.0
    qc_multi = frqi_circuit(stack, normalization=norm_multi)

    def _decode_multi(counts, _n=n, _norm=norm_multi):
        imgs = frqi_decode(counts, n=_n, m=1, normalization=_norm)
        # imgs is list of 2; return the green channel (index 1) for the reference comparison
        return imgs[1] if isinstance(imgs, list) else imgs

    recipes.append(CircuitRecipe(
        label=f"frqi_multi_n{n}", encoder="frqi_multi", n=n, q=0, m=1,
        qc=qc_multi,
        decoder=_decode_multi,
        reference=green.astype(np.float64),
    ))

    return recipes

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Run the qimp-mi encoder + GP suite on Aer (ideal + noisy) and optionally
on IBM Quantum hardware, with persisted artifacts and per-circuit metrics.

Designed for the IBM Quantum Open (free) plan: hardware execution is
restricted to a whitelist of high-value circuits (default: gp@1, gp@2,
frqi_multi@1) to stay well within the ~10 min/month QPU budget.

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import datetime as dt
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np


def _parse_hw_whitelist(raw: list[str]) -> set[tuple[str, int]]:
    """Parse '<encoder>@<n>' tokens, e.g. 'gp@2 frqi_multi@1'."""
    out: set[tuple[str, int]] = set()
    for tok in raw:
        if "@" not in tok:
            raise SystemExit(f"--hw-circuits expects '<encoder>@<n>', got {tok!r}")
        enc, n_str = tok.split("@", 1)
        out.add((enc.strip(), int(n_str)))
    return out


def _build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:

def _render_figure(outdir: Path, label: str, ref, panels: dict[str, "np.ndarray"]) -> None:
    """Render a side-by-side comparison figure for one (encoder, n).

    `panels` maps a pass name ('aer-ideal', 'aer-noisy', 'hw') to a decoded
    image array. The reference goes first; one |diff| panel per pass at the
    end."""
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    n_pass = len(panels)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 1 + 2 * n_pass, figsize=(3 * (1 + 2 * n_pass), 3))
    axes[0].imshow(ref, cmap="gray")
    axes[0].set_title("classical ref"); axes[0].axis("off")
    for i, (name, arr) in enumerate(panels.items()):
        axes[1 + 2 * i].imshow(arr, cmap="gray")
        axes[1 + 2 * i].set_title(name); axes[1 + 2 * i].axis("off")
        axes[2 + 2 * i].imshow(np.abs(arr.astype(np.float64) - ref.astype(np.float64)),
                                cmap="magma")
        axes[2 + 2 * i].set_title(f"|diff| {name}"); axes[2 + 2 * i].axis("off")
    (outdir / "figures").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    fig.tight_layout()

docs.title: 1. Motivation
docs.text:
The companion paper (paper/outline_qmi.docx, §7.4) flags hardware execution of the corrected GP circuit on a real IBM Quantum device as immediate future work — "doing so for n = 2 (six qubits) is within reach of current IBM Quantum hardware and would yield a fluorescence-microscopy GP image with quantified device noise." Today the library has a stub qimp.testing.device_test() that submits a single circuit to a Sampler v2 session, but nothing wires it to the encoder suite, no error mitigation is exposed, and there is no reproducible sweep that produces tables / figures.

This design specifies an end-to-end pipeline that produces, from a single command, the hardware analogue of the paper's Tables 2–3 and Figures 5–6 for the encoder suite (FRQI, FRQI-multi, NEQR, QPIE, MCRQI, NCQI) and the corrected GP circuit at n=1 and n=2, under the resource budget of the IBM Quantum Open plan (~10 min QPU/month, ≤3 active jobs).

docs.title: 2. User-visible deliverables
docs.text:
For a representative input image and --sizes 1 2:

  1. data/output/ibm/<UTC-timestamp>/summary.csv — one row per (encoder, n, pass) triple with shots, transpiled depth, 2q-gate count, PSNR/MSE/TV vs classical reference, wallclock seconds, job_id (when applicable).
  2. data/output/ibm/<UTC-timestamp>/figures/<encoder>_n<n>.png — 4 or 5 panels per circuit: classical reference, Aer-ideal decoded, Aer-noisy decoded, hardware decoded (when present), pixelwise |diff|.
  3. data/output/ibm/<UTC-timestamp>/runs/<encoder>_n<n>_<pass>/ — circuit.qpy, transpiled.qpy (HW only), counts.json, metadata.json. Full reproducibility from disk.
  4. data/output/ibm/<UTC-timestamp>/backend_info.json — name, qubit count, coupling map, basis gates, calibration timestamp.

All output paths are under data/, which is already gitignored.

docs.title: 3. Scope decisions (from brainstorming)
docs.text:
Decision Choice Rationale Circuit scope FRQI, FRQI-multi, NEQR, QPIE, MCRQI, NCQI, GP-corrected Full encoder + processing suite. NEQR/NCQI run with q=2 to stay NISQ-feasible. Spatial sizes n ∈ {1, 2} (sweep) n=2 is the paper's target (§7.4); n=1 is the small-size baseline. Mitigation Readout (TREX) + Dynamical Decoupling (XY4) Cheapest mitigation that meaningfully reduces depth/idle noise; no extra shots. ZNE deliberately excluded — budget too tight. Output PSNR table + figures + persisted artifacts + Aer-noise baseline All four boxes ticked in brainstorming. Plan IBM Quantum Open (free) ~10 min QPU/month, ≤3 active jobs, restricted backend list. HW vs Aer split Approach A — Aer ideal + Aer noisy on the full matrix; HW only for whitelisted circuits Maximum scientific signal within the Open budget. Whitelist: gp@n=1, gp@n=2, frqi_multi@n=1.

Circuits not in the HW whitelist run on Aer + NoiseModel.from_backend(...) only; their PSNR is the simulated-noise estimate rather than a measured device value. This limitation is acknowledged explicitly in the output report.

docs.title: 4. Architecture
docs.text:
scripts/run_hardware_sweep.py        ← CLI entry point
        │
        ▼
src/qimp/runtime/ibm.py              ← NEW: backend resolution, Sampler v2 wrapper,
                                       Aer-from-backend, persistence
        │
src/qimp/runtime/circuits.py         ← NEW: build_recipes(image, n) factory —
                                       one recipe per encoder
        │
src/qimp/testing.py                  ← unchanged; device_test() remains for
                                       back-compat (small refactor optional)
        │
data/output/ibm/<UTC-timestamp>/     ← all artifacts (gitignored)

The new modules live under src/qimp/runtime/ to match the existing pattern (runtime/simulator.py, runtime/memory_pool.py, etc.). No IBM-Runtime imports leak into processing/ or encoding/.

docs.title: 5.2 src/qimp/runtime/circuits.py
docs.text:
@dataclass
class CircuitRecipe:
    label: str                            # "frqi_n1", "gp_n2", ...
    encoder: str                          # "frqi" | "frqi_multi" | "neqr" | "qpie" | "mcrqi" | "ncqi" | "gp"
    n: int
    q: int                                # for NEQR/NCQI; 0 otherwise
    m: int                                # selection qubits; ≥1 for GP/MCRQI
    qc: QuantumCircuit
    decoder: Callable[[Counts], np.ndarray]
    reference: np.ndarray                 # classical target (same shape as decoded)

def build_recipes(
    image: np.ndarray, *, n: int, alpha: float = 0.5, q: int = 2,
) -> list[CircuitRecipe]:
    """One recipe per encoder.

    - `image` is the source frame. Downsampled to 2^n × 2^n (LANCZOS).
    - Two-channel encoders (FRQI-multi, MCRQI, GP): channels = (R, G) of `image`.
    - Single-channel encoders (FRQI, NEQR, QPIE, NCQI): channel = grayscale `image`.
    - NEQR/NCQI use q=2 by default (NISQ-friendly).
    """

The recipe factory is also the single source of truth for "what is a (encoder, n) reference image" — the classical comparison.

docs.title: 5.3 scripts/run_hardware_sweep.py
docs.text:
qimp-hw-sweep
  --image data/immagini/<file>.tif
  --sizes 1 2
  --shots 4096
  --backend ibm_brisbane              # optional; default: least-busy
  --hw-circuits gp@1 gp@2 frqi_multi@1   # whitelist; default = these three
  --outdir data/output/ibm
  --skip-hw                              # only Aer ideal + Aer noisy
  --list-backends                        # diagnostic, exits after printing

Execution order: Pass 1 Aer ideal → Pass 2 Aer noisy → Pass 3 hardware. Whitelisted (encoder, n) pairs go through all three passes; others only Aer.

Pre-Pass-3 safety check: estimate sum_jobs(depth × shots × avg_gate_time) and print expected QPU consumption. If above 120 s, require interactive confirmation. (Open plan has 10 min/month; 120 s is a soft warning, not a hard cap.)

Hardware submissions are sequential — the Open plan caps ≤3 active jobs and queues are long; serial submission keeps the pipeline simple and predictable.

docs.title: 6. Data flow
docs.text:
For each (encoder, n):

  1. build_recipes(image, n) materialises qc, decoder, reference.
  2. Pass 1 (Aer ideal): exact_counts(qc) → decode → metrics vs reference → persist_run("aer-ideal").
  3. Pass 2 (Aer noisy): aer_noisy_run(qc, backend) → decode → metrics → persist_run("aer-noisy").
  4. Pass 3 (HW, whitelist only):
  5. Transpile under optimization_level=3.
  6. Write metadata.json with job_id and status="submitted" to runs/<label>_hw/ before waiting.
  7. sampler.run([transpiled], shots=...) with TREX+DD; await with timeout_s.
  8. On success: update metadata.json (status="completed"), write counts.json, transpiled.qpy. Decode → metrics → summary.csv row.
  9. On timeout: keep metadata.json with job_id; log warning; move on. Recovery via separate qimp-hw-recover --job-id <id> script (out of scope for v1; see §10).

A per-run figure is generated lazily at the end: panels = classical | aer-ideal | aer-noisy | hw (if present) | |diff|.

docs.title: 7. Error handling
docs.text:
Credentials. Missing ~/.qiskit/qiskit-ibm.json or expired token → explicit error with token-refresh instructions; no silent fallback.

Backend. Named backend not found → list service.backends(operational=True) and abort. least_busy returns nothing matching min_qubits → abort with the same listing.

Transpile. Failures rethrown with (encoder, n, backend_name) context. No fallback to lower optimization_level (silent quality regression worse than abort).

Submission. Per-circuit try/except around sampler.run(...); one circuit failing does not abort the sweep. Job ID is persisted to disk before awaiting the result, so a wait-side crash leaves the job recoverable.

Decode. Existing decoders already default to 0.5 for pixels with zero total counts. Post-decode validation: shape correct, finite values, range plausible. Mismatch logged as decode_warning in the row; sweep continues.

Metrics. PSNR on a constant image is well-defined in qimp.metrics.psnr (verify in implementation; patch if needed).

Idempotency. Pre-execution, list runs/*/ already containing non-empty counts.json and skip them. Allows incremental re-runs without restarting from scratch.

Out-of-budget. Pre-Pass-3 cost estimate; soft warning at 120 s; interactive confirmation required before submission.

docs.title: 8. Testing
docs.text:
Three levels:

Unit (tests/unit/, always): - test_runtime_ibm.py — mock QiskitRuntimeService and SamplerV2. Cover: pick_backend (named + least-busy paths), persist_run (4 files, QPY round-trip), metadata.json is written before any wait, is_run_complete idempotency. - test_runtime_circuits.py — for each encoder in the suite, build_recipes produces a circuit with the correct num_qubits for (n, q, m) and a decoder that round-trips through exact_counts to an array of shape (2^n, 2^n).

Integration local (tests/integration/, always, no special marker): - test_sweep_aer_only.py — runs the script with --skip-hw --sizes 1 on a synthetic 4×4 image. Asserts: summary.csv has 2 × 7 = 14 rows; per-row Aer-ideal PSNR is above a generous floor (catches broken encoders); figures exist and are non-trivial.

Hardware (tests/hardware/, marker hardware, excluded from CI): - test_hw_smoke.py — minimal GP run at n=1, 4 qubits, 1024 shots, on least_busy of the Open plan. Asserts: job_id non-empty; counts decoded; PSNR ≥ 5 dB. End-to-end ratification, not a quality test.

Test markers are already declared in pyproject.toml (hardware, slow, gpu).

docs.title: 9. Performance and budget envelope
docs.text:
Rough estimates (Open plan, single backend, end of 2025 / start of 2026):

Run Qubits Transpiled depth (est.) Shots QPU time (est.) FRQI-multi n=1 4 ~150 4096 ~0.5 s GP n=1 4 ~250 4096 ~1 s GP n=2 6 ~1500 4096 ~6 s

Total QPU: ~8 s per full sweep, well under the 10-minute monthly budget. The dominant cost is queue wall-clock, which can be hours per submission on busy days — irrelevant to the budget but a UX concern. Hence sequential submission with persisted job_id.

docs.title: 10. Out of scope (deferred)
docs.text:
• ZNE / PEC mitigation. Excluded by brainstorming (budget). Trivial to add later: extra SamplerOptions block.
  • qimp-hw-recover recovery script. Will be added if the v1 timeout path triggers in practice. The infrastructure is already there: job_id is on disk.
  • Multi-backend comparison. Single backend per sweep. A multi-backend report would be a higher-level wrapper.
  • Pulse-level / fractional-gate optimisation. Default Qiskit transpile only.
  • Paper figure regeneration. The script produces figures/<encoder>_n<n>.png; integrating them into paper/joss_paper.md is a downstream task.

docs.title: 11. Open questions (none blocking)
docs.text:
• The Open plan's available backend list changes over time. The --list-backends mode is the runtime answer.
  • IBM may change SamplerOptions syntax across qiskit-ibm-runtime minor versions. Pin a known-good version range (>=0.28,<0.32 initial guess) in the implementation phase; verify against the version actually present in the user's environment.
